Task: Write a quick note explaining why TCP differs from UDP.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) differs from UDP (User Datagram Protocol) primarily in how each handles reliability, ordering, and connection management. TCP is connection-oriented: before data can flow, the two endpoints perform a three-way handshake to establish a session. During transmission, TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges received segments, retransmits lost ones, and applies congestion-control algorithms. All of this guarantees that data arrive intact, in order, and without duplication, but it adds latency and overhead. UDP, by contrast, is connection-less and offers a “best-effort” service: it simply wraps data in datagrams and sends them off. There are no built-in acknowledgments, retransmissions, or flow-control mechanisms, so applications that need those features must implement them themselves (or accept occasional loss or reordering). The trade-off is that UDP has far lower overhead and latency, making it well-suited for real-time traffic such as voice, video, or online gaming where speed matters more than perfect reliability.
